body:
Dermatologist explains the number one physiological reason mature skin turns dry, wrinkly, and fragile: Trans-Epidermal Water Loss (TEWL).

Imagine your skin cells are like bricks, and your natural oils (lipids) are the mortar holding them together. 

In your 20s and 30s, that mortar is thick and strong. But as estrogen drops after 40, your body stops producing those natural lipids.

The "mortar" crumbles. Your skin barrier develops microscopic cracks and holes. Dermatologists call this a compromised lipid barrier, leading to severe Trans-Epidermal Water Loss (TEWL). 

Essentially, your skin can no longer hold onto hydration, water literally evaporates out of your body into the air all day long. 

This "leaky skin" is what causes that sudden, drastic shift to a paper-thin, deflated, and intensely wrinkled texture.

body:
I need to tell you about the lotion lie.

For years, I believed that winter dry skin just needed more moisture. More lotion. More cream. Applied more often.

So every winter, I'd buy the thickest, richest body butter I could find. Apply it religiously. Morning, night, sometimes in between.

And every winter, my skin got worse anyway.

At 56, after menopause, my winter skin had become unbearable.

My legs would crack so badly they'd bleed. My arms had this rough, sandpaper texture that caught on my sweaters. My hands were so dry they’d sting when I washed them.

I'd spend $40–50 a month on heavy creams and body butters. Layer them on like frosting.

And still wake up feeling like my skin had turned to paper overnight.

I thought something was wrong with me. That my skin was just broken. That I'd have to suffer through every winter for the rest of my life.

Then I learned the truth about why lotion doesn't work on menopausal skin in winter.

It's not about moisture.
It's about moisture RETENTION.

After menopause, your skin barrier is damaged. It has tiny gaps that let water escape constantly.

In summer, this is annoying.
In winter — with cold air outside and dry heat inside — it's devastating.

Your skin is hemorrhaging moisture 24/7.

And lotions?
They're water-based. They add moisture to the surface. But they can't seal those gaps.

So the moisture evaporates. Sometimes within an hour.

That “tight” feeling you get after moisturizing?
That's the water leaving your skin.

You're not under-moisturizing.
Your products literally cannot keep moisture in.

But oils work differently.

Oils penetrate through your damaged barrier and actually seal it from the inside. They create a protective layer that stops moisture from escaping.

It's not about adding more.
It's about keeping in what you have.

I switched to Goda Silk Body Oil six weeks ago. Right at the start of winter.

First week: My skin stopped feeling tight by noon. First time in years.
Second week: The cracks on my legs started healing. The sandpaper texture on my arms started softening.
Fourth week: I realized I hadn't bought body lotion in a month. Hadn't needed it.

One application in the morning.
Skin stays hydrated all day.
No reapplying. No layering products. No cracking, bleeding, or flaking.

I wore a skirt with bare legs to a holiday party last week. In December. Without being self-conscious about how my skin looked.

My husband said my legs looked amazing.
I almost didn’t believe him.

This is the first winter since menopause that my skin hasn't been a constant source of frustration and embarrassment.

One oil. Applied once a day. That's all it took.

Goda Silk Body Oil actually seals in moisture instead of letting it evaporate.

If you've been drowning your skin in lotion every winter and still suffering… it's not you.
It's that lotions can't do what oils can.

Stop the lie.
Start the oil.
Your winter skin will thank you. 💛

body:
This is why your neck, arms, and legs suddenly look crepey and thin, and it has nothing to do with "just getting older."

Let me be direct.

If you've noticed your skin developing that thin, crinkled texture that looks like crepe paper... if your neck has those horizontal lines you never had before... if your arms and legs look deflated and saggy instead of firm... if you're covering up body parts you used to show confidently...

You've probably been told it's "just part of aging" or "what happens after 50."

Maybe you've tried expensive firming creams. Maybe they helped temporarily. Maybe they did nothing at all.

But here's what no dermatologist is telling you:

The problem isn't that your skin is aging. It's not that you need "tightening treatments."

It's that menopause has triggered a catastrophic collapse in the structural proteins holding your skin up, and without them, your skin literally cannot maintain its architecture.

According to research published in dermatology journals, women lose up to 30% of their skin's collagen content in the first five years after menopause, with an additional 2% loss every year after that.

Collagen and elastin are the scaffolding that keep your skin firm, tight, and smooth.

Without them, your skin loses its ability to hold its shape, creating the thin, wrinkled, saggy appearance that makes you look decades older than you feel.

Here's exactly how estrogen decline destroys the structural integrity of your skin:

When estrogen levels drop during menopause, your fibroblasts, the cells responsible for producing collagen and elastin, essentially shut down.

Without estrogen stimulation, these cells stop creating the proteins that give your skin strength, elasticity, and the ability to bounce back.

Studies show that the decrease in collagen, elastin, and hyaluronic acid causes increased skin rigidity and decreased elasticity, leading to the characteristic crepey texture and sagging you're seeing in the mirror.

The skin literally thins, both the outer epidermis and the deeper dermis become significantly thinner, making your skin appear translucent and fragile.

But it gets worse.

Research on menopausal skin shows that estrogen decline doesn't just stop collagen production, it actively accelerates collagen breakdown:

* Fibroblast activity drops dramatically, reducing your skin's ability to repair and regenerate
* Elastin fibers fragment and degrade, eliminating the elasticity that kept your skin tight
* The subcutaneous fat layer thins, removing the padding that supported your skin from underneath
* Hyaluronic acid levels plummet, causing your skin to lose its ability to retain moisture and plumpness

Without these structural components functioning normally, your skin collapses like a tent with its poles removed.

The firmness disappears. The smooth surface wrinkles. The elasticity vanishes.

And here's the part that will shock you:
